sections.section_title: Introduction to The Unit Impulse Input

image_slots.image_description: A clean left-to-right block diagram. On the left, show an input arrow labeled $x(t)=\delta(t) with a small unit impulse spike at t=0$. The arrow enters a rectangle labeled LTI system. On the right, show an output arrow leaving the block, labeled response to $\delta$(t), with a simple generic waveform. Keep the visual limited to the unshifted unit impulse case. Do not include convolution, signal decomposition, shifted impulses, scaled impulses, or the notation $h(t)$.

blocks.text: An LTI system is useful because linearity and time invariance let one response pattern be reused. The first input used to expose that pattern is the unit impulse, written $\delta(t)$.
Here $\delta(t)$ is an idealized unit impulse located at $t=0$. In this section, treat it as the input signal being applied to the system, not as a normal finite-height pulse and not as the output.
Applying $\delta(t)$ to an LTI system is the standard probe case. The system takes that impulse input and produces an output response to the unit impulse at the origin.

That output is the reference response for this system. Later sections will use the same reference response when the impulse input is shifted or scaled, but this section only identifies the unshifted unit impulse input and the response it produces.

image_slots.image_description: A single instructional figure with five small labeled input-signal panels feeding the same LTI system. Panel A is labeled $x_A(t)=\delta(t) and shows a unit impulse spike at t=0$. Panel B is labeled $x_B(t)=u(t) and shows a unit step$. Panel C is labeled $x_C(t)=\delta(t-2) and shows an impulse spike at t=2$. Panel D is labeled $x_D(t)=2delta(t) and shows an unshifted impulse spike annotated with weight 2$. Panel E is labeled $x_E(t)=rectangular pulse and shows a short finite-width pulse$. Include a shared note saying candidate inputs to the same LTI system. Do not show outputs, convolution, $h(t)$, or shifted/scaled response patterns.

example_content.example_prompt: Identify the probe input in a set of candidate signals sent into the same LTI system: $\delta(t)$, $u(t)$, $\delta(t - 2)$, 2$\delta$(t), and a rectangular pulse.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the phrase probe input. In this lesson, the probe input must be the unshifted unit impulse: it has to be an impulse, it has to be located at $t=0$, and it has to be the unit impulse rather than a scaled impulse.

Read the candidate labels first. The unit step $u(t)$ is not an impulse, and the rectangular pulse is a finite-width pulse, so neither one is the unit impulse probe. The shifted impulse $\delta(t - 2)$ is an impulse, but it is located at $t=2$ instead of $t=0$. The scaled impulse 2$\delta$(t) is at $t=0$, but it is not the unit impulse because it has a factor of 2.

The only candidate that passes all three checks is $\delta(t)$: it is an impulse, it is located at $t=0$, and it is the unit impulse. Therefore $\delta(t)$ is the canonical probe input for this LTI system.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing the Impulse Input from Its System Output

image_slots.image_description: A clean left-to-right block diagram. On the left, an input arrow labeled $x(t)=\delta(t) enters a rectangle labeled LTI system$; near the input label, show a small unit impulse spike at $t=0$. On the right, an output arrow leaves the rectangle and is labeled $y(t)$; near the output label, show a distinct non-impulse response waveform such as a smooth decaying curve. Make arrow direction unambiguous. Do not show $h(t)$, convolution, shifted impulses, scaled impulses, or response-template annotations.

example_content.example_prompt: A block diagram shows $\delta(t)$ entering an LTI system and a waveform $y(t)$ leaving it. Identify which signal is the impulse input and which signal is the system output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the direction of the arrows through the system block. The signal on the arrow entering the LTI system is the input applied to the system, and the signal on the arrow leaving the system is the output produced by the system.
Start with the entering arrow. Its label is $\delta(t)$, so $\delta(t)$ is the impulse input probe. This is the signal being applied to the system, not the response generated by the system.

Now read the leaving arrow. The waveform labeled $y(t)$ is the system output produced after the input $\delta(t)$ passes through the LTI system. The output waveform may have a different shape from the impulse, but its role is still output, not input.

sections.section_title: Using the Unit Impulse Output as the Reference Response

image_slots.image_description: A clean left-to-right block diagram. On the left, an input arrow labeled $x(t)=\delta(t) enters a rectangle labeled LTI system$; near the input label, show a small unit impulse spike at $t=0$. On the right, an output arrow leaves the rectangle and is labeled $r(t)$; near the output label, show a distinct non-impulse response waveform. Add a small annotation next to $r(t)$ that says reference response for later impulse inputs. Do not show shifted impulses, scaled impulses, convolved outputs, convolution notation, or $h(t)$.

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system produces the output $r(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t)$. Interpret what role $r(t)$ will play for later shifted and scaled impulse inputs.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the input-output pair: the input is $\delta(t)$, and the corresponding output is $r(t)$. Since $\delta(t)$ is the unshifted unit impulse probe, the output produced by that probe is the response pattern tied to this LTI system.
First confirm the applied input. The diagram says the system is driven by $\delta(t)$, so this is the standard unit impulse probe case rather than a step input, shifted impulse, or scaled impulse.

Now read the output produced by that probe. The signal $r(t)$ is not the input and it is not arbitrary; it is the output generated by this system when the input is the unit impulse. In this lesson, that makes $r(t)$ the reference response for later impulse-input reasoning.

Later shifted and scaled impulse inputs will reuse this reference response pattern. For now, the required interpretation is only that the output caused by the unit impulse input is the system's reference response.

prompt_blocks.text: Which candidate is the unshifted unit impulse probe input?

choice_blocks.text: $\delta(t - 2)$
$\delta(t)$
2 $\delta(t)$
rectangular pulse

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The probe input is the unshifted unit impulse. Only $\delta(t)$ is both an impulse and located at $t = 0$ with unit weight. The step, shifted impulse, scaled impulse, and rectangular pulse all fail one of those checks.

prompt_blocks.text: Which candidate is the canonical probe input?

choice_blocks.text: 3 $\delta(t)$
rectangular pulse
$\delta(t + 1)$
$\delta(t)$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The canonical probe input is $\delta(t)$. It is the only option that is an impulse, is unshifted, and has unit weight. The other choices each change one feature of the probe input, such as amplitude, shift, or signal type.

On the right, an output arrow labeled $r(t)$ leaves the block and points to a distinct smooth decaying response waveform. Make the arrow directions unambiguous. Do not show $h(t)$, convolution, shifted impulses, or scaled impulses.

At the bottom, a downward output arrow labeled $y(t)$ exits the block and points to a distinct smooth decaying response waveform. Make the input and output directions unambiguous. prompt_blocks.text: A block diagram shows $\delta(t)$ entering an LTI system and $r(t)$ leaving it. Which statement correctly identifies the input and output?

choice_blocks.text: $r(t)$ is the input and $\delta(t)$ is the output.
$\delta(t)$ is the input and $r(t)$ is the output.
The LTI system block is the output signal.
Both signals are inputs.
$r(t)$ is unrelated to $\delta(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: $\delta(t)$ is the input and $r(t)$ is the output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The arrow entering the system carries the applied input, so $\delta(t)$ is the probe signal. The arrow leaving the system carries the output produced by that input, so $r(t)$ is the system response.

prompt_blocks.text: A block diagram shows $\delta(t)$ entering an LTI system and $y(t)$ leaving it. Which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: $\delta(t)$ is the output and $y(t)$ is the input.
The LTI system block is the output signal.
Both arrows carry input signals.
$\delta(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output.
$y(t)$ is the impulse input and $\delta(t)$ is the output.

questions.correct_answer: $\delta(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal on the entering arrow is the applied input, and the signal on the leaving arrow is the response produced by the system. The label $y(t)$ names the output, while $\delta(t)$ names the impulse input probe.

sections.section_title: Using the Unit Impulse Output as the Reference Response

image_slots.image_description: A clean left-to-right block diagram. On the left, an input arrow labeled $\delta$(t) enters a rectangle labeled LTI system. On the right, an output arrow labeled $r(t)$ leaves the block and points to a distinct smooth response waveform. Add a light annotation next to $r(t)$ that says reference response for later impulse inputs. Do not show shifted impulses, scaled impulses, or convolution notation.

A clean top-to-bottom block diagram. At the top, an input arrow labeled $\delta$(t) points downward into a rectangle labeled LTI system. At the bottom, an output arrow labeled $g(t)$ points downward out of the block and leads to a distinct smooth response waveform. Add a light annotation next to $g(t)$ that says reference response for later impulse inputs. Do not show shifted impulses, scaled impulses, or convolution notation.

prompt_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the input $\delta(t)$ produces the output $r(t)$. What is the correct interpretation of $r(t)$ in this lesson?

choice_blocks.text: $r(t)$ is the input signal rather than the output.
$r(t)$ is arbitrary and cannot be reused for the system.
$r(t)$ already represents the response to a shifted impulse.
$\delta(t)$ itself is the reference output.
$r(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: $r(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is the unit impulse $\delta(t)$, and the signal leaving the system is the output. In this lesson, that output is not just any response; it is the reference response that later impulse inputs will reuse.

prompt_blocks.text: A different LTI system produces $g(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t)$. What does $g(t)$ represent here?

choice_blocks.text: $g(t)$ is the input signal rather than the output.
$g(t)$ is arbitrary and cannot be reused for the system.
$g(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.
$g(t)$ already represents the response to a shifted impulse.
A step input, rather than a unit impulse input, defines this reference response.

questions.correct_answer: $g(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The symbol can change, but the role does not. If $\delta(t)$ produces $g(t)$, then $g(t)$ is the output tied to the unit impulse probe, so it serves as the reference response for later impulse-input reasoning.
